failures.title: Mercedes-Benz OM605 Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Stretch and Guide Wear - All variants
items.whatHappens: The timing chain and plastic guide rails can stretch and wear over high mileage, leading to a distinct rattling noise on cold starts. If ignored, the chain can jump a tooth, causing valve-to-piston contact and catastrophic engine failure.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, a timing chain and guide kit replacement is straightforward and cost-effective. If the engine has already suffered valve damage, a full reconditioned unit is the only viable path.

items.title: Injector Seal Weeping ("Black Death") - All variants
items.whatHappens: The copper washer seals at the base of the injectors degrade over time, allowing combustion gases to escape. This creates a black, crusty carbon buildup around the injector heads and can lead to difficult cold starts or rough idling.
items.repairVsReplace: This is a routine maintenance item, not a terminal failure. Replacing the seals and cleaning the cylinder head is inexpensive and should be done preventatively.

items.title: Glow Plug and Pre-chamber Issues - High-mileage units
items.whatHappens: As a pre-chamber diesel, the OM605 relies heavily on the glow plug system for cold starts. Failed glow plugs can lead to extended cranking, which in turn can cause the pre-chambers to crack or the glow plugs to seize in the cylinder head.
items.repairVsReplace: Glow plug replacement is routine, but if a plug has seized and broken off in the head, cylinder head removal or replacement is often required.

failures.goodYearsLine: The OM605 is widely regarded as one of Mercedes’ most robust inline-6 diesels, offering a significant refinement step up from the 5-cylinder OM602 it replaced. Units maintained with regular oil changes and preventative injector seal replacements routinely exceed 300,000 miles without major internal issues .

variants.title: OM605 Sub-Codes Explained - Which One Is in Your Car?
variants.intro: ═══════════════════════════════════════ INTRO: The OM605 family shares the same fundamental 2.5L inline-6 block and pre-chamber head design, but forced induction and tuning vary depending on the chassis. Identifying your exact sub-code ensures you order the correct injection pump, turbo, and ancillary components. - Fitted to: E-Class W124 (E 250 D), E-Class W210 (E 250 D) - Key technical difference: The base naturally aspirated variant, featuring a simpler ancillary layout without turbo plumbing and a mechanical injection pump calibrated for lower output. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; no unique widespread defects beyond standard high-mileage wear. - Interchange note: Not a straight swap with the .960 turbo variants; the injection pump, exhaust manifold, and oil return lines differ significantly. - Fitted to: Select export W124/W210 models and specific commercial applications - Key technical difference: Functionally identical to the .910 in core architecture, but calibrated for specific regional emission standards or fitted with different ancillary brackets (e.g., alternator or vacuum pump orientation). - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above. - Interchange note: Directly interchangeable with the OM605.910 in most applications, provided the injection pump and ancillary brackets are swapped to match the original chassis specification. - Fitted to: E-Class W124 (E 250 TD), E-Class W210 (E 250 TD), G-Class W463 (G 250 TD) - Key technical difference: Adds a turbocharger and intercooler to the 2.5L block, requiring a higher-capacity mechanical injection pump, revised piston cooling jets, and an upgraded cooling system to handle the additional heat. - Sub-code-specific failure note: Shares the family failure pattern above; turbocharger shaft wear and vacuum pump leaks are the primary additional wear items. - Interchange note: Can be swapped with the .910/.950 block, but requires the complete turbo kit, different injection pump, and revised engine management linkages.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement OM605 Engine - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used OM605 engine makes sense only if it comes with verifiable service history and a recent timing chain guide inspection. Given the age of these vehicles, the primary risk is hidden corrosion or degraded rubber seals, so a compression test is mandatory before purchase.

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: A proper reconditioned OM605 engine is the sweet spot for most buyers. A reputable rebuild will address the common failure points by fitting a new timing chain guide kit, updated injector seals, and a refreshed mechanical injection pump, giving the engine a fresh lease on life.

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full OM605 engine rebuild is justified for high-mileage G-Class applications or classic W124/W210 restorations where originality and maximum longevity are required. An upgraded rebuild should include line-boring the block, new pistons/rings, and a balanced crankshaft.

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Sourcing and fitting through our vetted network ensures your OM605 engine is installed by specialists familiar with classic Mercedes mechanical diesels, backed by a nationwide warranty.
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: Because the OM605 is typically found in vehicles valued between £1,500 and £8,000 for standard examples (though classic low-mileage W124 and G-Class models can command much higher premiums), a full replacement can represent a significant portion of the car's worth. If the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value, evaluate scrap value before committing .

items.answer: A reconditioned Mercedes OM605 engine typically costs between £1,600 and £2,600 for supply only . Fitted costs generally range from £2,400 to £3,600 depending on the specialist, while used units can be found from £500 but carry higher risk due to the engine's age. → Compare OM605 engine replacement quotes today

items.question: What is the most common failure on the OM605 engine?
items.answer: The most documented issues are timing chain stretch and guide wear, alongside injector seal weeping and glow plug failures. Timing chain rattle on cold starts is the primary warning sign of guide degradation, which can lead to catastrophic valve damage if ignored, whereas injector seal failure causes black carbon buildup around the injector heads but is a cheap and routine fix. → Get quotes for a rebuilt OM605 with these issues resolved

items.question: Which Mercedes models use the OM605 engine?
items.answer: The OM605 was fitted to the W124 E-Class (E 250 D, E 250 TD), the W210 E-Class (E 250 D, E 250 TD), and the W463 G-Class (G 250 TD), serving as the definitive 6-cylinder diesel for these mid-size and off-road chassis throughout the mid-1990s. → Check your registration to confirm your exact OM605 fitment

items.question: Should I buy a used or reconditioned OM605 engine?
items.answer: A reconditioned OM605 is strongly recommended over a used unit due to the age of these vehicles. A proper rebuild will replace the timing chain, plastic guide rails, tensioner, and injector seals, eliminating the most common failure points, whereas used engines may appear cheaper upfront but often hide stretched chains that will fail shortly after installation. → Compare reconditioned OM605 engine prices from UK specialists

items.question: What is the difference between OM605.910, .950, and .960?
items.answer: The OM605.910 is the 2.5L naturally aspirated variant, the OM605.950 is a 2.5L naturally aspirated version calibrated for specific export or commercial applications, and the OM605.960 is the 2.5L turbocharged version. The .960 requires a higher-capacity mechanical injection pump, revised piston cooling jets, and an upgraded cooling system to handle the additional heat and cylinder pressures. → Enter your reg above to identify your exact OM605 sub-code ═══════════════════════════════════════
